client: I've been having a really hard time since my sister passed away six months ago. It was a car accident, completely out of nowhere, and I just... I can't seem to find any reason to enjoy anything anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: What you're carrying right now — the sudden, devastating loss of your sister — is one of the heaviest things a person can experience, and the exhaustion and emptiness in your voice tells me just how much this has worn you down. It makes complete sense that joy feels unreachable right now, and I want you to know that simply showing up here today, even with doubt, took real courage. We don't need to have all the answers right away — we can just start by making space for what you're going through, together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Thank you for saying that, I guess. It's just... I keep waiting to feel something other than this hollow, heavy feeling, and it hasn't lifted at all in six months, so part of me wonders if "making space" for it is really going to help or if it'll just keep me stuck in it longer. I don't really know how sitting here and talking is supposed to make any of this better.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a tension in your voice — tells me there's a real urgency to this fear that you might be stuck like this forever, and that's an incredibly painful place to sit. That thought, *"nothing will ever change,"* is actually one of the most common and convincing lies that grief and depression tell us, and it's worth gently questioning whether six months of pain is truly evidence that relief is impossible, or whether it's evidence of how much you loved her. Talking won't erase the loss, but it can slowly help us loosen the grip those heavy thoughts have on you — not by avoiding the grief, but by learning to carry it differently.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about it being evidence of how much I loved her, and some part of me wants to hold onto that, but it also feels a little... I don't know, like a reframe that's too neat, too easy? Because the truth is I also feel this guilt that I can't shake, like I was supposed to call her that weekend and I didn't, and no amount of reframing that into "proof of love" really touches that feeling. It just sits there, heavy and separate from everything else.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that — and the fact that you did tells me you're being really honest with yourself, which takes courage. That guilt you're describing is its own separate wound, and it deserves to be looked at directly rather than smoothed over. Can we sit with that for a moment — because that thought, *"I was supposed to call and I didn't,"* is carrying an enormous weight, and I'd gently want to ask: what do you think your sister would have believed about you, based on everything she knew of you, not just that one weekend?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I know she probably wouldn't have blamed me, she wasn't like that, she was actually the more forgiving one between the two of us. But when I try to think about what she would have said, I just feel this wall come up, like I don't deserve to give myself that comfort, you know? It almost feels like letting myself off the hook too easily, and I'm not sure I've earned that yet.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just said — you already *know* what your sister would have said, but there's a part of you that's decided you don't deserve to receive it yet, almost like the guilt has become a way of staying close to her, or of punishing yourself enough to feel like the loss is accounted for. I notice even as you said it, there was a kind of tightness there — like you were speaking quickly, trying to get through something painful. That belief, *"I haven't earned the right to forgive myself,"* isn't a truth about what you deserve — it's grief talking, and it's worth asking: if your sister were the forgiving one, would she ever set a condition on her love for you that you had to suffer first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because no, she wouldn't have done that, that's just not who she was. But then I feel this other thing come up, like... maybe the problem isn't really about her at all, maybe it's that I don't trust myself to forgive myself without it meaning I'm just moving on and forgetting her. Like if I let go of the guilt, I'm somehow letting go of her too, and I'm not ready for that.
therapist: The way you just said that — quickly, at a higher pitch, like the words were almost rushing out ahead of you — tells me you've just touched something really core, and it sounds like a breakthrough moment even if it feels frightening. What you've uncovered is so important: the guilt hasn't just been about that missed call, it's been doing a job — keeping her close, keeping you connected to her. And I want to gently offer this: forgiving yourself and remembering her with love aren't opposites — releasing guilt doesn't mean releasing *her*, it might actually free you to carry her with you in a way that feels more like her, warm and forgiving, rather than this heavy, punishing weight.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually... lands differently than the other things you've said, and I'm not sure if that scares me or gives me a tiny bit of relief, maybe both at the same time. But I don't really know how to carry her in that warmer way you're describing, like practically speaking, what does that even look like day to day? It feels like a beautiful idea but also kind of abstract, and I'm worried I'll just slip back into the guilt because at least that feels familiar and concrete.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, at a higher pitch, with that mix of fear and the tiniest flicker of hope — tells me this idea is genuinely landing somewhere real in you, even if it feels fragile and unfamiliar. You're right that guilt feels concrete, and we can absolutely make the alternative just as concrete: it might look like pausing when something reminds you of her — a song, a meal she loved — and instead of pushing it away or drowning in guilt, letting yourself say *"she would have liked this,"* and allowing that to be a moment of connection rather than loss. We can build those small, specific anchors together, so that carrying her warmly becomes something you practice in real moments rather than just a beautiful idea.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of those small moments, and there are actually things that remind me of her all the time, like she loved this specific kind of terrible reality TV that I always made fun of her for watching. But I'm a little scared that if I try to do that intentionally, like as a practice, it'll feel forced or performative, and then I'll feel guilty about that too, like I'm not grieving her the right way.
therapist: There's something quietly beautiful happening right now — even as your words carry worry, your voice has a softness and warmth to it when you talk about her and that terrible reality TV, like a small light coming through. That image of her watching it, and you teasing her, *that's* her — and I'd gently challenge the idea that there's a "right way" to grieve, because that belief is just another form of the same guilt trying to stay in charge. What if watching one episode of that show wasn't performative, but just... you, being someone who loved her and letting yourself feel that for an hour?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I could actually do that, like it doesn't feel as impossible as some of the other things we've talked about today. But I'm already anticipating that I'll sit down to watch it and either cry the whole way through and feel worse, or not cry at all and then feel guilty for not crying, like I can't even imagine a version where it just... goes okay. Is it normal to be this worried about something that's supposed to be comforting?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me your mind is already racing ahead, trying to pre-solve every possible way this could go wrong — which is actually your anxiety trying to protect you from being hurt, and that makes complete sense given how much pain you've been carrying. But notice what you're doing: you're setting up a situation where *any* response you have — crying, not crying — becomes evidence against yourself, which means you've built a trap with no good exit. What if instead, the only thing the evening needs to "go okay" is that you showed up for her at all — and whatever you feel while you're there is just the right feeling for that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing of "showing up for her" actually feels more manageable than trying to grieve correctly, and I notice something loosened a little in my chest just hearing it. But I guess I'm also aware that I've had moments before where I thought I was ready to do something like this and then completely avoided it at the last minute, so I don't fully trust myself to follow through. How do I actually make myself do it when the moment comes and everything in me wants to just close the laptop and walk away?
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with that high pitch — tells me even imagining that moment of avoidance brings up real anxiety, but I also heard something important: you said something *loosened* in your chest, and that's not nothing, that's your body responding to something true. When the moment comes and you want to close the laptop, you don't have to convince yourself to grieve — you just have to do one tiny thing, like pressing play before you're ready, because readiness rarely comes first, action does. It might help to make it even smaller and more concrete: maybe you text someone beforehand and say "I'm going to watch one episode tonight" — not to perform grief, but to make it real enough that walking away feels like a choice rather than just something that happens to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The texting idea actually makes sense to me in a way I didn't expect, like it adds a kind of weight to the intention that just thinking about it doesn't have. But I'm realizing I don't really have anyone I'd feel comfortable texting about this, most of my friends have kind of stopped checking in after the first couple of months, and I don't want to burden the few who are still around. So that part feels lonelier than I expected it to.
therapist: There's a real ache in what you just shared, and I can hear it — your voice carries a kind of exposed vulnerability, like you reached for something and found an unexpected emptiness there. That loneliness, the way people slowly drifted after the first few weeks, is one of the quietest and most painful parts of grief, and the thought that reaching out would burden someone says a lot about how much you're used to carrying this alone. I want you to know that what you just named — that you *want* connection but don't feel safe enough to ask for it — is something we can work on together, and for now, you could even text *me* about it, meaning: write it down, say it out loud to yourself, make it real — because you deserve at least one witness to what you're carrying, even if we're still building that circle.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech
